front: What are the three energy systems?
back: I. The aerobic system 2. The ATP-PC system 3. The anaerobic glycolytic system.

front: What determines which energy system the body uses during exercise?
back: The intensity and duration of the exercise

front: Which energy systems are used during high-intensity activity?
back: Anaerobic energy systems — specifically the ATP-PC system and the anaerobic glycolytic system.

front: When is the aerobic system predominantly used?
back: During low-intensity

front: What is the only usable form of chemical energy in the body?
back: ATP is the only usable form of chemical energy in the body.

front: How is energy from food used to form ATP?
back: Food is broken down to release energy

front: What is ATP made up of?
back: One molecule of adenosine and three phosphate groups.

front: How is energy released from ATP?
back: Energy is released by breaking the bonds that hold the ATP compound together.

front: What enzyme is used to break down ATP and what does it form?
back: ATPase breaks down ATP into ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi)

front: Why does the body need to constantly rebuild ATP?
back: Because ATP is broken down to release energy

front: How can ATP be re-synthesised in the body?
back: Through three different types of chemical reactions that occur in the muscles.

front: What fuels the resynthesis of ATP in the muscles?
back: Either food or a chemical called phosphocreatine (PC)

front: What type of exercise does the aerobic system support?
back: Low-intensity

front: What does the aerobic system break glucose down into?
back: Carbon dioxide and water.

front: How efficient is the aerobic system when oxygen is present?
back: It is very efficient and can produce a high yield of ATP.

front: How many molecules of ATP can be produced from the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule?
back: Up to 38 molecules of ATP.

front: Besides glucose
back: what other fuels can the aerobic system use?

front: What is produced when fats and proteins are broken down in the aerobic system?
back: Acetyl coenzyme A.

front: What is the role of acetyl coenzyme A in the aerobic system?
back: It enters the Krebs Cycle

front: What are the three stages to the aerobic system?
back: I.Glycolysis 2.Krebs cycle 3.Electron transport chain

front: Where does glycolysis take place?
back: In the sarcoplasm of the muscle cell.

front: In which types of respiration does glycolysis occur?
back: Glycolysis occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

front: What is the current focus of glycolysis in the aerobic system?
back: Its role when oxygen is readily available.

front: What fuels can glycolysis use?
back: Glycogen/glucose

front: How many molecules of ATP are produced by glycolysis?
back: 2 molecules of ATP.

front: What is the role of the Link Reaction in aerobic respiration?
back: It transfers energy from glycolysis to the Krebs Cycle but is not considered a formal stage of aerobic respiration.

front: What are the products at the end of glycolysis?
back: 2 molecules of ATP and pyruvic acid.

front: What happens to pyruvic acid before entering the Krebs Cycle?
back: It is oxidised into two acetyl groups.

front: How are the acetyl groups transported into the Krebs Cycle?
back: They are carried by coenzyme A

front: Where does the krebs cycle take place?
back: In the matrix of the mitochondria

front: Where do the two acetyl groups go after the Link Reaction?
back: They diffuse into the matrix of the mitochondria.

front: What do the acetyl groups combine with in the Krebs Cycle?
back: Oxaloacetic acid.

front: What compound is formed when acetyl groups combine with oxaloacetic acid?
back: Citric acid.

front: What happens to citric acid during the Krebs Cycle?
back: Hydrogen is removed from the citric acid.

front: How many ATP molecules are produced during the Krebs Cycle?
back: 2 ATP molecules.

front: Where is the hydrogen from the Krebs Cycle transported to?
back: It is taken to the electron transport chain.

front: What happens to the carbon released during the Krebs Cycle?
back: It forms carbon dioxide

front: What carries hydrogen into the Electron Transport Chain (ETC)?
back: Hydrogen carriers transport hydrogen into the ETC.

front: Where does the Electron Transport Chain occur?
back: In the cristae of the mitochondria.

front: What happens to hydrogen in the ETC?
back: It splits into hydrogen ions and electrons

front: What happens to hydrogen ions in the ETC?
back: They are oxidised to form water

front: What role do hydrogen electrons play in the ETC?
back: They provide the energy needed to re-synthesise ATP.

front: How many ATP molecules are produced during the Electron Transport Chain?
back: 34 molecules of ATP.

front: What is the total yield of ATP?
back: 38 molecules of ATP

front: What is a key advantage of the aerobic system in terms of ATP yield?
back: It produces a high yield — up to 38 molecules of ATP from one molecule of glucose.

front: Why is the aerobic system considered efficient in terms of by-products?
back: It produces no fatiguing by-products.

front: Why can the aerobic system support long-duration exercise?
back: The body has large stores of glycogen and triglycerides

front: What is a major disadvantage of the aerobic system in terms of activation time?
back: It is a complicated system that cannot be used immediately; it takes time for oxygen to become available.

front: Why is the breakdown of fatty acids less efficient than glycogen in the aerobic system?
back: Fatty acid transport to muscles is slower and requires 15% more oxygen to break down than glycogen.

front: Besides carbohydrates, what other macronutrients can be used to make energy?
back: Fat and protein (though you only need to know the basic fact about protein, not how it's used).

front: How is stored fat broken down for transport in the blood?
back: It is broken down into glycerol and free fatty acids.

front: What is beta oxidation?
back: A process where fatty acids are converted into acetyl coenzyme A.

front: What happens to acetyl coenzyme A from fat metabolism?
back: It enters the Krebs Cycle, following the same pathway as glycogen metabolism.

front: How does the ATP yield from fat compare to glucose?
back: More ATP can be made from one molecule of fatty acid than from one molecule of glucose.

front: In what type of exercise are fatty acids the predominant energy source?
back: Long-duration, low-intensity exercise like a marathon.

front: What determines when the body begins using fat instead of glucose for energy?
back: The fitness level of the performer.

front: What happens to fat breakdown if the fitness of the performer is increased?
back: Fat oxidisation happens earlier as they can supply more oxygen sooner and can delay glycogen usage for later in the performance.

front: Why is fat breakdown less efficient than glucose breakdown?
back: Because fat breakdown requires more oxygen than glucose breakdown (this is a limitation).

front: Why can't fat be used for fast, explosive exercise?
back: Fat cannot be used without oxygen, making it unsuitable for anaerobic activity.

front: Why might fat stores be a disadvantage during exercise despite their energy value?
back: They must be carried as excess non-functional weight, requiring more energy to complete any task.

front: Why is carbohydrate still necessary even when using fat for energy?
back: Because fat breakdown requires carbohydrates to keep the Krebs Cycle functioning.

front: What happens to glycogen stores during prolonged, continuous exercise?
back: They become depleted, slowing down the breakdown of fats.

front: How does glycogen depletion affect the Krebs Cycle and ATP resynthesis?
back: The Krebs Cycle slows, which reduces the rate of ATP resynthesis.

front: What term do marathon runners often use to describe the effects of glycogen depletion?
back: "Hitting the wall."

front: How does the anaerobic glycolytic (lactic acid) system compare to the ATP-PC system?
back: It provides energy for high-intensity activity for longer than the ATP-PC system.

front: What factors determine how long the anaerobic glycolytic system can last?
back: The individual's fitness level and the intensity of the exercise.

front: How long does the anaerobic glycolytic system last when working flat out to exhaustion?
back: Only a short time (30secs-3mins).

front: How long can the anaerobic glycolytic system last when working at a slightly reduced intensity?
back: Around 2-3 minutes.

front: Is the lactic acid system aerobic or anaerobic?
back: It is always an anaerobic process, even when part of aerobic respiration.

front: Where does the lactic acid system take place?
back: In the sarcoplasm of the muscle cell when oxygen is not available.

front: What process provides energy in the lactic acid system?
back: Anaerobic glycolysis, which releases energy to resynthesise ATP.

front: What is the net ATP yield of the lactic acid system from 1 molecule of glucose?
back: 2 ATP (4 are produced, but 2 are used during glycolysis).

front: What is the first step of anaerobic glycolysis?
back: Glucose (or glycogen) is broken down by enzymes like glycogen phosphorylase and phosphofructokinase.

front: What is produced from glucose during anaerobic glycolysis?
back: Pyruvic acid and a net of 2 ATP molecules.

front: What happens to pyruvic acid if oxygen is not available?
back: It is converted into lactic acid by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.

front: What is the final product of anaerobic glycolysis when oxygen is limited?
back: Lactic acid (lactate).

front: What is an advantage of the anaerobic glycolytic system?
back: ATP can be re-synthesised quite quickly due to very few chemical reactions, and it lasts longer than the ATP-PC system.

front: How can lactic acid be used when oxygen is present?
back: It can be converted back into liver glycogen or oxidised into CO₂ and H₂O to be used as fuel.

front: What is a disadvantage of the anaerobic glycolytic system?
back: Lactic acid is a by-product that denatures enzymes and prevents them from increasing the rate of chemical reactions.

front: Why does anaerobic glycolysis release less energy than aerobic respiration?
back: Only a small amount of energy (5%) is released from glycogen under anaerobic conditions compared to 95% under aerobic conditions.

front: When is the anaerobic glycolytic system useful?
back: It can be used for a sprint finish to produce an extra burst of energy.

front: What fuel does the ATP-PC system use?
back: Phosphocreatine (PC).

front: What type of activity is the ATP-PC system used for?
back: High-intensity, short-duration activities.

front: Where is phosphocreatine (PC) found in the muscle?
back: In the sarcoplasm as an energy-rich phosphate compound.

front: How does PC help resynthesise ATP?
back: PC breaks down quickly to release energy that resynthesises ATP from ADP + Pi.

front: Why is the ATP-PC system's rapid availability important?
back: It provides immediate energy for a single maximal effort.

front: Give examples of activities that rely on the ATP-PC system.
back: Long jump take-off and shot put throw.

front: What is the main limitation of the ATP-PC system?
back: PC stores are limited and only last about 5-8 seconds.

front: When can phosphocreatine (PC) be replenished?
back: During low-intensity exercise when oxygen is available.

front: Why does Usain Bolt slow down in the last 20m of a 100m sprint?
back: His PC stores are depleted, so he must switch to slower energy systems.

front: Is the ATP-PC system aerobic or anaerobic?
back: It is an anaerobic process.

front: What enzyme detects high levels of ADP to trigger ATP resynthesis in the ATP-PC system?
back: Creatine kinase.

front: What happens when phosphocreatine (PC) is broken down?
back: It splits into phosphate (Pi), creatine (C), and energy.

front: How is energy from PC breakdown used in the ATP-PC system?
back: The energy is used in a coupled reaction to convert ADP + Pi into ATP.

front: What is a coupled reaction in the ATP-PC system?
back: It's when energy released from PC breakdown is transferred to resynthesise ATP.

front: What does an ATP molecule consist of?
back: Adenosine + 3 phosphates (ATP = Adenosine-P-P-P).

front: What does creatine kinase do when ADP levels are high?
back: It triggers the breakdown of phosphocreatine (PC) to resynthesise ATP.

front: During the first few seconds of exercise, which energy system is relied on almost exclusively?
back: The ATP-PC system, using ATP stores in the muscles.

front: Why does the body switch to other energy systems after the first few seconds of exercise?
back: Because ATP and PC stores are limited and quickly become exhausted.

front: What happens if exercise continues at a high intensity?
back: PC stores may only partially replenish, as there isn't enough energy for creatine and Pi to reform PC.

front: Why can't ATP stores fully replenish during high-intensity exercise?
back: The high rate of ATP breakdown through other energy systems prevents full resynthesis of ATP in the muscles.

front: How quickly can ATP be re-synthesised in the ATP-PC system?
back: ATP can be re-synthesised rapidly.

front: How quickly can phosphocreatine (PC) stores be replenished?
back: 50% replenished in 30 seconds, 100% replenished in 3 minutes.

front: What is a major advantage of the ATP-PC system in terms of by-products?
back: It produces no fatiguing by-products.

front: How can the duration of the ATP-PC system be extended?
back: Through creatine supplementation, which increases PC availability.

front: What is the main limitation of phosphocreatine (PC) in the ATP-PC system?
back: There is only a limited supply of PC in the muscle cell.

front: How many ATP molecules are produced per PC molecule in the ATP-PC system?
back: Only 1 ATP can be re-synthesised for every 1 PC.

front: When can PC re-synthesis occur?
back: Only in the presence of oxygen, during reduced-intensity exercise.

front: The full run through
back: Creatine kinase detects high levels of ADP. This triggers the breakdown of PC into ADP and Pi, which releases energy. This energy is used in a coupled reaction to turn ADP and Pi into ATP. This ATP is used in the muscles.

front: Do all three energy systems contribute during physical activity?
back: Yes, all three energy systems contribute during all types of activities.

front: What determines which energy system is predominant?
back: The intensity and duration of the activity.

front: How do energy systems work during a game with constantly changing intensity?
back: There will be a mix of all three energy systems depending on the demands at each moment.

front: What type of respiration do slow twitch fibres mainly use for ATP production?
back: Aerobic respiration.

front: What type of respiration do fast twitch fibres mainly use for ATP production?
back: Anaerobic respiration.

front: How many ATP molecules are produced per glucose in aerobic respiration?
back: Up to 38 ATP.

front: How many ATP molecules are produced per glucose in anaerobic respiration?
back: 2 ATP.

front: Why is anaerobic respiration less efficient than aerobic respiration?
back: It produces fewer ATP per glucose and leads to lactic acid build-up, causing quicker fatigue.

front: What is the ATP-PC/anaerobic-glycolytic threshold?
back: The point at which the ATP-PC system is exhausted and the anaerobic glycolytic system takes over, around 10 seconds

front: What is the anaerobic glycolytic/aerobic threshold?
back: The point at which the anaerobic glycolytic system is exhausted and the aerobic system takes over, around 3 minutes

front: Why are slow twitch fibres more fatigue-resistant?
back: They rely on aerobic respiration, which is more efficient and sustainable for low to medium intensity activity.

front: Why do fast twitch fibres fatigue more quickly?
back: They rely on anaerobic respiration, which is faster but inefficient and causes lactic acid accumulation during high-intensity activity.

front: What is the main pathway for ATP production in slow-twitch fibres?
back: The aerobic system.

front: What is the main pathway for ATP production in fast-twitch fibres?
back: The lactate anaerobic system during glycolysis.

front: How efficient is ATP production in slow-twitch fibres?
back: Very efficient, producing up to 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

front: How efficient is ATP production in fast-twitch fibres?
back: Not efficient, only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

front: How quickly is ATP produced in slow-twitch fibres?
back: Production is slow but sustainable.

front: How quickly is ATP produced in fast-twitch fibres?
back: Production is fast but cannot last long.

front: Why do slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue?
back: They are endurance-based and use aerobic energy pathways.

front: Why do fast-twitch fibres fatigue quickly?
back: They rely on anaerobic ATP production and have the least resistance to fatigue.

front: What energy systems are used during short-duration/high-intensity exercise?
back: Mainly the ATP-PC system and the anaerobic glycolytic (lactate) system.

front: How long can the ATP-PC system last?
back: Approximately 8-10 seconds.

front: How long can the anaerobic glycolytic system last?
back: Up to around 3 minutes depending on intensity.

front: How long does energy production last for a 400m runner?
back: Around 45-60 seconds, mainly anaerobic glycolytic.

front: Why is a 400m runner exhausted at the end of the race?
back: Due to lactic acid build-up causing fatigue and requiring a long recovery period.

front: How long does energy production last for an 800m runner?
back: Around 1 minute 40 seconds to 2 minutes, mainly anaerobic glycolytic.

front: Why can an 800m runner sustain activity longer than a 400m runner?
back: Because the energy demand is slightly lower, allowing the system to last longer.

front: What is the chemical formula for lactic acid?
back: C₃H₆O₃.

front: What happens when lactic acid breaks down?
back: It dissociates, releasing hydrogen ions (H⁺).

front: What compound forms when the remaining lactate combines with sodium or potassium ions?
back: The salt lactate.

front: What causes increased acidity in the muscles?
back: The accumulation of hydrogen ions from lactic acid dissociation.

front: How does increased acidity affect performance?
back: It slows down enzyme activity, reducing glycogen breakdown and causing muscle fatigue.

front: What happens to the lactate produced in the muscles?
back: It diffuses into the blood, where blood lactate levels can be measured.

front: What is the lactate threshold?
back: The point during exercise at which lactate rapidly accumulates in the blood (about 2 mmol above resting levels).

front: What is OBLA?
back: Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation — the point when blood lactate levels exceed 4 millimoles per litre.

front: What causes OBLA to occur?
back: When the body cannot produce enough oxygen to break down lactate, leading to its accumulation.

front: How are lactate threshold and OBLA related?
back: They are different ways of measuring the same physiological point where lactate builds up rapidly.

front: What does measuring OBLA indicate?
back: It gives an indication of endurance capacity.

front: Why can some people delay when the lactate threshold occurs?
back: Because they can work at higher intensities before OBLA due to better endurance adaptations.

front: How is lactate threshold expressed?
back: As a percentage of VO₂ max.

front: What happens to the lactate threshold as fitness increases?
back: It becomes delayed, meaning the athlete can sustain higher intensities before fatigue.

front: What percentage of VO₂ max is the lactate threshold for average performers?
back: Around 50-60% of VO₂ max.

front: What percentage of VO₂ max is the lactate threshold for elite performers?
back: Up to 90% of VO₂ max.

front: How much does training affect VO₂ max?
back: Training has little impact since VO₂ max is largely genetically determined.

front: How does training improve performance if VO₂ max doesn't change much?
back: It delays the lactate threshold, allowing the athlete to perform at higher intensities for longer.

front: What is the relationship between fitness and lactate threshold?
back: The fitter you are → higher lactate threshold → later fatigue → can work harder.

front: What test is a good example to illustrate OBLA?
back: The multi-stage fitness test (bleep test).

front: Why does the multi-stage fitness test become more demanding over time?
back: Because the time allowed to complete each shuttle decreases.

front: What happens when the performer can no longer provide energy aerobically?
back: They rely on anaerobic systems to resynthesise ATP.

front: What happens to lactate levels during the multi-stage fitness test?
back: They increase as intensity rises, leading to muscle fatigue.

front: Why does the performer eventually slow down or stop in the multi-stage fitness test?
back: Because lactate accumulation causes fatigue, preventing them from keeping up with the bleeps.

front: What are the five factors affecting the rate of lactate accumulation.
back: 1-Exercise intensity 2-Fitness of the performer 3-Muscle fibre type 4-Rate of blood lactate removal 5-Respiratory exchange ratio (RER)

front: What happens to lactate production at low to moderate intensities?
back: The aerobic system meets most ATP demand, so lactate production is low and balanced with removal (~1-2 mmol·L⁻¹).

front: What happens to lactate production as exercise intensity increases?
back: More reliance on anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate faster than the body can remove it.

front: How does aerobic fitness affect lactate accumulation?
back: More aerobically fit athletes have adaptations that slow lactate accumulation.

front: What adaptations help delay lactate accumulation in trained athletes?
back: Increased mitochondrial density, oxidative enzyme activity, and capillarisation in muscle.

front: How does increased mitochondrial density affect lactate accumulation?
back: It allows more pyruvate to be used aerobically instead of being converted to lactate.

front: How does capillarisation affect lactate accumulation?
back: It improves oxygen delivery and removal of metabolic byproducts like lactate and hydrogen ions.

front: How do Type I (slow-twitch) fibres influence lactate accumulation?
back: They have high oxidative capacity and produce less lactate because they rely mainly on aerobic metabolism.

front: How do Type II (fast-twitch) fibres influence lactate accumulation?
back: They rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis and produce more lactate per unit of work.

front: When does lactate build up more rapidly?
back: When more fast-twitch fibres are recruited, such as during sprinting or explosive movements.

front: What determines the net accumulation of lactate?
back: The balance between lactate production and lactate removal.

front: How can lactate be removed from the body?
back: It can be oxidised for fuel, converted back to pyruvate, or turned into glucose via the Cori cycle in the liver.

front: What factors improve lactate removal?
back: Active recovery, greater mitochondrial capacity, more capillaries, efficient lactate transporters, and better buffering.

front: What is the Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER)?
back: The ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed — used to determine which fuel (fat or carbohydrate) is being used.

front: What does an RER close to 1.0 indicate?
back: High carbohydrate metabolism, which leads to greater glycolysis and higher lactate production.

front: What does an RER closer to 0.7 indicate?
back: Predominant fat oxidation, which is slower, more aerobic, and produces minimal lactate.

front: How does RER change as exercise intensity increases?
back: It rises, indicating greater carbohydrate use and faster lactate accumulation.

front: What does VO₂ max measure?
back: The maximum amount of oxygen the body can take in, transport, and use per minute during exercise.

front: How much of VO₂ max is genetically determined?
back: Around 75%.

front: How much can training improve VO₂ max?
back: By approximately 10-20%.

front: Why does training have a limited effect on VO₂ max?
back: Because it is largely determined by genetics.

front: What does aerobic training do to VO₂ max?
back: It allows the body to take up and use more oxygen more efficiently.

front: What effect does an increased number and size of mitochondria have on VO₂ max?
back: Increases the muscles' ability to use oxygen for aerobic energy production, improving VO₂ max.

front: What effect does an increased surface area of alveoli have on VO₂ max?
back: Allows more efficient gas exchange, increasing oxygen uptake and improving VO₂ max.

front: What effect does increased maximum cardiac output have on VO₂ max?
back: Increases the amount of blood pumped per minute, improving oxygen delivery to working muscles and VO₂ max.

front: How does training affect VO₂ max?
back: Aerobic training can improve VO₂ max by up to 10-20% by increasing the body's ability to take in, transport, and use oxygen.

front: How do genetics affect VO₂ max?
back: Genetics largely determine VO₂ max potential — up to 75% of VO₂ max is genetically inherited, limiting possible improvement through training.

front: How does age affect VO₂ max?
back: VO₂ max decreases with age as the body becomes less efficient; this decline can be slowed but not stopped through regular exercise.

front: How does gender affect VO₂ max?
back: Males generally have a higher VO₂ max than females due to greater muscle mass and haemoglobin levels; in trained athletes, the gap reduces to about 10%.

front: How does body composition affect VO₂ max?
back: A higher body fat percentage reduces VO₂ max because fat tissue is not oxygen-demanding, lowering overall aerobic efficiency.

front: How does lifestyle affect VO₂ max?
back: Smoking, inactivity, poor diet, and low fitness reduce VO₂ max, while a healthy, active lifestyle helps maintain or improve it.

front: What are all the factors affecting VO2 max?
back: 1-genetics 2-training 3-number and size of mitochondria 4-surface area of alveoli 5-maximum cardiac output 6-age 7-gener 8-body composition 9-lifestyle

front: What is indirect calorimetry used to measure?
back: It measures energy expenditure.

front: What gases does indirect calorimetry measure?
back: The amount of CO₂ produced and O₂ consumed at rest and during aerobic exercise.

front: What does calculating gas volumes reveal?
back: Whether fat or carbohydrate is being used as the main energy source.

front: What can indirect calorimetry precisely calculate?
back: VO₂ and VO₂ max.

front: What is one advantage of indirect calorimetry?
back: It is accurate for steady-state oxidative metabolism over short periods.

front: What is one disadvantage of indirect calorimetry related to equipment?
back: It requires a lot of equipment to be attached to the head.

front: Why can't indirect calorimetry measure anaerobic energy?
back: Because it only measures oxygen use and carbon dioxide production, which occur in aerobic metabolism.

front: What is one financial disadvantage of indirect calorimetry?
back: It is expensive, though cheaper than building a direct calorimetry chamber.

front: What does lactate sampling involve?
back: Taking a tiny blood sample and analysing it on a handheld device to measure lactate levels.

front: What does lactate sampling show?
back: The amount of lactate in the blood and the intensity of exercise.

front: What does a higher lactate threshold indicate?
back: The athlete is fitter and can work at a higher intensity before fatigue.

front: Why is lactate sampling useful?
back: It gives an indication of fitness levels.

front: How does lactate sampling help training?
back: It allows the performer to choose relevant training zones.

front: How can lactate sampling track progress?
back: It provides a baseline for comparison to see improvements over time.

front: What does a lower lactate level at the same exercise intensity suggest?
back: Improved peak speed/power, longer time to exhaustion, better recovery heart rate, and a higher lactate threshold.

front: What are some advantages of lactate sampling?
back: 1-equipment is accessible + cheap 2-equipment is portable 3-you can get results quickly

front: What are some disadvantages of lactate sampling?
back: -performer might be scared to use

front: What are some benefits of VO2 max testing?
back: 1-it has high validity 2-it is the primary measurement of your performance level 3-it can help influence training

front: What are some disadvantages of VO2 max testing?
back: 1-It can lack reliability 2-it can be uncomfortable for the performer 3-it is expensive for amateurs

front: What is a way avoid the expensive downsides?
back: A smart watch can calculate it roughly but it isn't as accurate

front: What happens to oxygen at altitude?
back: The percentage of oxygen in the air stays the same, but the partial pressure of oxygen decreases as altitude increases.

front: What happens to the diffusion gradient of oxygen at altitude?
back: It decreases, reducing oxygen diffusion between the air, lungs, and blood.

front: What happens to haemoglobin saturation at altitude?
back: Haemoglobin is not fully saturated because less oxygen diffuses into the blood.

front: What happens to oxygen delivery to muscles at altitude?
back: Less oxygen is delivered to the muscles, reducing aerobic performance and VO₂ max.

front: What protien is made as a result of altitude training?
back: erythropoietin (EPO)

front: What does EPO do?
back: Stimulates red blood cell production which contains haemoglobin that binds to O2 increasing oxygen carrying capacity.

front: What are the advantages of training at altitude?
back: Increased oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, increased aerobic endurance, and increased VO₂ max.

front: What are the disadvantages of training at altitude?
back: Loss of fitness/detraining, altitude sickness, benefits lost quickly after returning to sea level, limited EPO production, expensive and homesickness.

front: What is the overall impact of altitude on performance?
back: Initially, performance decreases due to reduced oxygen availability, but long-term adaptations can improve aerobic capacity.

front: What activities are involved in plyometric training?
back: Hopping, bounding, depth jumping, medicine ball work

front: What is the aim of plyometric training?
back: To develop power, speed, and explosive strength

front: Which muscle fibre type does plyometric training use?
back: Fast-twitch fibres (Type II)

front: What contraction occurs first in plyometric training?
back: Eccentric contraction

front: What contraction follows the eccentric phase in plyometrics?
back: amortisation phase

front: What is the amortisation phase?
back: the transition between the eccentric and concentric contraction

front: What happens during the amortisation phase?
back: - stretch reflex is activated - elastic energy is stored / held

front: Why is it important that the amortisation phase is extremely quick?
back: Shorter amortisation phase = more power

front: What happens if the amortisation phase is too slow?
back: If the phase is too long, the stored elastic energy dissipates as heat, reducing explosivness

front: What contraction follows the amortisation phase in plyometrics?
back: Concentric contraction

front: What reflex is activated during plyometric training?
back: The stretch reflex

front: Which receptors detect muscle stretch in plyometrics?
back: Muscle spindles

front: Where do muscle spindles send impulses during plyometrics?
back: To the spinal cord/CNS via afferent impulses

front: What type of energy is stored in the eccentric phase of plyometrics?
back: Elastic energy

front: What is the purpose of the stretch reflex in plyometrics?
back: To prevent overstretching and reduce injury risk

front: What is the three-phase mechanism used in plyometrics?
back: The stretch-shortening cycle

front: What are the three phases of the stretch-shortening cycle?
back: Pre-stretch, amortisation, muscle contraction

front: What is interval training?
back: Training involving periods of high-intensity exercise followed by rest or low-intensity exercise

front: What does HIIT stand for?
back: High-Intensity Interval Training

front: Which energy systems does HIIT improve?
back: Mainly anaerobic, with additional aerobic benefits

front: What is an example work-to-rest ratio in HIIT?
back: 20 seconds intense exercise, 10 seconds rest

front: How many cycles are typically used in HIIT?
back: 6-8 cycles

front: Give a physiological benefit of HIIT.
back: Increased anaerobic capacity

front: Give another benefit of HIIT.
back: Reduced body fat/obesity

front: Why is HIIT often motivational?
back: It uses short-duration, intense bouts of exercise

front: What does SAQ training involve?
back: Being coached in correct movement technique

front: Why does SAQ use progression exercises?
back: To improve motor abilities for faster, more accurate skill execution

front: What are the benefits of SAQ training?
back: Increased muscular power, improved kinaesthetic/spatial awareness, improved motor skills and reaction time
